findings.summary: March 3 2025: DOGE SSA member sent encrypted password-protected file containing names and addresses of ~1,000 people to DHS, copying DOGE adviser Steve Davis and a DOGE Department of Labor employee. SSA's CIO has been unable to access the file to determine its contents. Revealed in DOJ Notice of Corrections to Record (AFSCME v. SSA, D.Md.) filed January 16 2026.

Between March 7-17, 2025, DOGE SSA team members shared data through Cloudflare — a third-party server not approved for storing SSA data and outside SSA security protocols. On March 3, a DOGE SSA member sent an encrypted password-protected file with names and addresses of ~1,000 people to DHS, copying DOGE adviser Steve Davis and a DOGE DOL employee. SSA cannot access that file to determine contents. As of DOJ court filing (Jan 2026), SSA cannot determine if data still exists on Cloudflare.

On March 24 2025, a DOGE SSA team member signed a 'Voter Data Agreement' in his capacity as an SSA employee with an unnamed political advocacy group. The group's stated aim: find evidence of voter fraud and overturn election results in certain states. The group had acquired state voter rolls and sought to match them to SSA data to find noncitizens. SSA first discovered this agreement in November 2025 during an unrelated review. Two Hatch Act referrals made to Office of Special Counsel in December 2025. True the Vote published an 'Appeal to DOGE' in March 2025 and is suspected but denies involvement. No evidence SSA data was actually transferred to the advocacy group.

After Supreme Court lifted DOGE access ban (June 6 2025), DOGE employees transferred a live copy of the Social Security NUMIDENT database to a cloud server without independent security controls. NUMIDENT contains: SSNs for 300M+ Americans, names, addresses, dates/places of birth, parents' names. Aram Moghaddassi authorized the operation via July 15 2025 memo accepting security risks. SSA CDO Charles Borges filed whistleblower complaint August 26 2025 and resigned August 29 2025.

AFSCME AFL-CIO v. Social Security Administration (D.Md., CL:69664313) filed Feb 21 2025. March 20 2025: federal judge issued TRO blocking DOGE access to SSA data. June 6 2025: Supreme Court overturned the TRO, allowing DOGE access to resume. January 16 2026: DOJ filed Notice of Corrections to Court Record revealing misstatements in earlier court filings — DOGE had in fact been accessing SSA data and exfiltrating it to Cloudflare (unapproved third party). Democracy Forward moved for discovery and depositions on DOGE's unlawful SSA data access.

SpaceX v. NLRB constitutional conflict: Elon Musk's DOGE accessed NLRB case management data (NxGen) in March 2025 while SpaceX has pending NLRB cases (19-CA-309274) and Musk is pursuing constitutional challenge to NLRB structure. The NLRB NxGen data exfiltrated includes trade secrets, witness testimony, and ongoing case data. Fifth Circuit dismissed SpaceX's appeal for lack of jurisdiction March 2025; constitutional challenge continues. Over a dozen federal court cases involve DOGE data access questions per NPR.

curation.lead:
The Social Security Administration is a federal independent agency that administers retirement, disability, and survivor benefits for approximately 70 million Americans. Its systems hold some of the most sensitive personal data in the federal government: the NUMIDENT database alone contains Social Security Numbers, names, addresses, dates and places of birth, parents' names, and citizenship information for every person ever issued an SSN — more than 548 million records.

Beginning in February 2025, personnel operating under the banner of DOGE embedded at SSA and obtained read-write access to core agency systems including PSSNAP and NUMIDENT. Between March 7 and 17, 2025, DOGE-affiliated staff routed SSA data through Cloudflare — a commercial server neither approved for SSA data nor subject to agency security protocols. On March 3, a DOGE SSA member transmitted an encrypted, password-protected file containing names and addresses of approximately 1,000 individuals to DHS, copying DOGE adviser Steve Davis and a DOGE Department of Labor employee. As of the DOJ's January 16, 2026 Notice of Corrections to the court record, SSA's Chief Information Officer had been unable to access the file or determine whether the Cloudflare data was ever deleted [Finding #6404] [Finding #6432].

On March 24, 2025, a DOGE SSA team member signed a 'Voter Data Agreement' as an SSA employee with an unnamed political advocacy group seeking to match SSA records against state voter rolls to identify noncitizens. SSA first discovered the agreement in November 2025 during an unrelated records review. Two Hatch Act referrals were forwarded to the Office of Special Counsel in December 2025. No evidence has emerged that SSA data was transferred to the advocacy group [Finding #6410].

After the Supreme Court lifted a preliminary injunction on June 6, 2025, DOGE personnel requested a live production copy of the NUMIDENT database within four days. On June 25, the full database was uploaded to an Amazon Web Services test cloud environment outside SSA's verified security controls. SSA's own internal risk assessment, dated June 16, had found a 35–65 percent probability of a data breach with catastrophic adverse effect. Aram Moghaddassi, the DOGE-aligned SSA CIO, issued a Provisional Authorization to Operate on July 15, 2025 with the written justification: 'I have determined the business need is higher than the security risk.' SSA Chief Data Officer Charles Borges filed a whistleblower complaint with the Office of Special Counsel on August 26, 2025, and resigned three days later [Finding #6407] [Finding #6395] [Finding #6397] [Finding #6401] [Finding #6431].
curation.system_role: SSA functioned as the primary federal repository for citizen identity data targeted during the DOGE access period. The agency's institutional role made it valuable on two distinct axes: its payment infrastructure (monthly disbursements to 70 million beneficiaries) and its identity infrastructure (NUMIDENT as a master record linking SSNs to names, addresses, birth data, and immigration status). The DOGE penetration of SSA illustrates how a nominally administrative agency becomes a high-value intelligence and enforcement asset when its records can be cross-referenced with immigration enforcement, voter roll matching, or commercial identity systems. The pattern at SSA — DOGE-aligned personnel installed as CIO, career officials sidelined or removed when they objected, data moved to unapproved commercial infrastructure, the agency unable to account for what was copied or where it went — was documented by the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee minority staff as a cross-agency template, not an isolated incident.

sections.title: Early Access and Cloudflare Data Transfer
sections.content:
DOGE personnel arrived at SSA in February 2025. Aram Moghaddassi was hired as a Department of Labor Policy Advisor on February 18, detailed to SSA on February 22, and gained read-write access to the SSA PSSNAP system on March 14. The sequence from arrival to write access to a core benefits system took less than four weeks [Finding #6462].

Between March 7 and 17, 2025, DOGE-affiliated SSA staff shared agency data through Cloudflare servers. Cloudflare is a commercial content delivery and network services company; it had not been approved as a storage or transit environment for SSA data and operated outside SSA's security authorization framework. On March 3 — before the main Cloudflare window — one DOGE SSA member sent an encrypted, password-protected file containing names and addresses of approximately 1,000 people to DHS. The transmission copied Steve Davis, a DOGE adviser, and a DOGE Department of Labor employee. SSA's CIO was unable to open the file. As of January 16, 2026, when the Department of Justice filed a Notice of Corrections to the court record in AFSCME v. SSA, the agency could not determine whether the data transmitted through Cloudflare had been deleted [Finding #6404] [Finding #6432].

The DOJ's January 2026 notice acknowledged that earlier government representations to the court had been inaccurate: DOGE had in fact been accessing SSA data and routing it through the unapproved Cloudflare infrastructure during the period when the government had represented otherwise [Finding #6414].

sections.title: Voter Data Agreement
sections.content:
On March 24, 2025, a DOGE SSA team member signed a 'Voter Data Agreement' in his capacity as an SSA federal employee. The agreement was with an unnamed political advocacy group whose stated objective was to identify evidence of voter fraud and contest election results in specific states. The group had acquired state voter rolls and sought to match them against SSA records to identify noncitizens who had voted [Finding #6410].

SSA did not discover the agreement until November 2025, when a routine records review surfaced it. Two Hatch Act referrals were submitted to the Office of Special Counsel in December 2025. The Hatch Act prohibits federal employees from using their official authority to interfere with or affect the result of an election or from engaging in certain political activities while on duty. True the Vote, a Texas-based organization that published an 'Appeal to DOGE' in March 2025 focused on noncitizen voter detection, has been identified as a suspected — but unconfirmed — party to the agreement. True the Vote has denied involvement. No evidence has emerged that SSA records were actually transferred to the advocacy group under the agreement [Finding #6410].

Separately, Aram Moghaddassi emailed the deputy chief of staff for Florida Governor Ron DeSantis from a DHS email account in March 2025, requesting Florida voter registration and voting data. The email stated: 'On our end, Florida voter registration and voting data would be helpful immediately to check for voter fraud.' The email was obtained via public records request by American Oversight. No evidence has emerged that Florida voter rolls were shared in response [Finding #6475] [Finding #6450].

sections.title: NUMIDENT Database Transfer to AWS
sections.content:
The NUMIDENT (Numerical Identification System) is SSA's master identity database. It contains SSNs, names, phone numbers, addresses, dates and places of birth, citizenship status, race and ethnicity, and parents' names and SSNs for every person who has been issued a Social Security Number — more than 300 million living Americans and an additional population of deceased persons. Total SSNs issued exceeded 548.3 million as of early August 2025 [Finding #6413].

After a federal district court issued a temporary restraining order on March 20, 2025, blocking DOGE access to SSA data, the Supreme Court lifted that injunction on June 6, 2025. On June 10–11, DOGE staffer John Solly formally requested authorization to copy the live NUMIDENT database to a cloud environment. The request came four calendar days after the Supreme Court ruling. On June 16, SSA's own internal Risk Assessment Form concluded that a NUMIDENT copy to cloud storage carried a 35–65 percent probability of a data breach with a catastrophic adverse effect rating [Finding #6395] [Finding #6516].

Despite that assessment, the upload proceeded. On June 25, 2025, DOGE personnel transferred a live production copy of the NUMIDENT to an Amazon Web Services virtual private cloud test environment. Authorization for the upload was obtained from DOGE-aligned SSA official Michael Russo on June 25. The environment had not undergone the verified security controls required for SSA production data. No audit process or oversight external to DOGE-affiliated staff was documented [Finding #6397] [Finding #6431].

Aram Moghaddassi, who had been appointed SSA CIO following Michael Russo's brief tenure, issued a Provisional Authorization to Operate for the cloud environment on July 15, 2025. His written justification, quoted directly in court records: 'I have determined the business need is higher than the security risk.' [Finding #6401] The Senate HSGAC minority staff report — the Peters report, released September 26, 2025 — documented the full authorization sequence and cited this language. The report assessed that a worst-case NUMIDENT breach could require re-issuing Social Security Numbers for all 548 million-plus Americans, with cascading effects on banking, employment, healthcare, and housing, and would expose the data to foreign adversaries including Russia, China, and Iran [Finding #6413].

SSA CDO Charles Borges filed a whistleblower disclosure with the Office of Special Counsel on August 26, 2025, specifically naming the NUMIDENT cloud transfer as an unlawful act. He resigned August 29, 2025. The Peters report identified SSA as part of a cross-agency pattern in which career cybersecurity officials who raised objections were sidelined or removed, and DOGE-affiliated personnel were installed as CIOs to approve DOGE staffers' access without following standard oversight procedures [Finding #6407] [Finding #6409].

sections.title: Death Master File Operation
sections.content:
On April 8, 2025, SSA added more than 6,300 living immigrants to the Death Master File — a federal database used by financial institutions, employers, and government agencies to verify whether an individual is deceased. For this operation SSA renamed the file the 'Ineligible Master File.' The list of individuals was provided by DHS and comprised immigrants whose temporary legal status had recently been revoked. The additions were recorded with synthetic, fabricated death dates. The population included minors; at least one was 13 years old [Finding #6476].

The authorization chain ran from Aram Moghaddassi, who transmitted the DHS list to SSA, through Acting Commissioner Leland Dudek, who signed two memoranda with DHS Secretary Kristi Noem authorizing the operation. Dudek signed despite initially concluding the action was illegal. Career SSA IT chief Greg Pearre was physically removed from his office when he refused to execute the plan on the same grounds [Finding #6476].

Moghaddassi had characterized the 6,300 individuals as immigrants 'homeland security officials had identified as having temporary legal status but who were now either on the terrorist watch list or had FBI criminal records.' The Death Master File additions, if not reversed, would have caused those individuals' benefits, bank accounts, and government services to be suspended or terminated based on fabricated records of death [Finding #6476].

sections.title: Litigation: AFSCME v. SSA and Related Proceedings
sections.content:
AFSCME AFL-CIO v. Social Security Administration (D. Md., CourtListener docket CL:69664313) was filed February 21, 2025. On March 20, 2025, the district court issued a temporary restraining order blocking DOGE access to SSA systems and data. On June 6, 2025, the Supreme Court vacated the TRO, allowing DOGE access to resume — a ruling that DOGE personnel used within four days to initiate the NUMIDENT cloud copy request [Finding #6414] [Finding #6516].

On January 16, 2026, the Department of Justice filed a Notice of Corrections to the Court Record, acknowledging that earlier representations to the court had been inaccurate. The government's prior filings had misstated the extent and nature of DOGE's access to SSA data; the notice acknowledged that DOGE had accessed SSA data and routed it through Cloudflare — a commercial, unapproved server — during the March 7–17, 2025 window. Democracy Forward, as counsel for AFSCME, moved for discovery and depositions regarding DOGE's unlawful SSA data access following the corrected filing [Finding #6414].

The Senate Finance Committee separately demanded answers from SSA after the January 2026 court filing revealed the agency could not account for the full extent of data accessed and shared by DOGE personnel. The Peters HSGAC minority staff report (September 26, 2025) documented SSA as one of multiple agencies where DOGE operations likely violated the Privacy Act of 1974, the E-Government Act of 2002, FISMA, the Federal Records Act, and potentially the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act [Finding #6408].

The NLRB data-access conflict — in which DOGE accessed NLRB case management data (NxGen) while SpaceX had pending NLRB cases and Elon Musk was pursuing a constitutional challenge to NLRB's structure — illustrates the broader pattern of DOGE data access intersecting with concurrent commercial and legal interests of DOGE-affiliated private parties. The Fifth Circuit dismissed SpaceX's NLRB appeal for lack of jurisdiction in March 2025; the constitutional challenge continued. More than a dozen federal court cases involved DOGE data access questions as of NPR's April 2025 reporting [Finding #6440].

sections.title: Key Personnel
sections.content:
Aram Moghaddassi was the central DOGE-affiliated figure at SSA. Born February 1999, he graduated from UC Berkeley with a BS in Applied Mathematics in 2021 and worked at Neuralink (2021–2022) and X Corp/Twitter (December 2022 through early 2025). He held simultaneous appointments at SSA and DHS during the DOGE period, was the fourth CIO at SSA since January 20, 2025, and personally authorized both the NUMIDENT cloud transfer and granted DOGE members access to USCIS immigration verification systems. He was one of two SSA staffers referred for Hatch Act violations in December 2025 in connection with the Voter Data Agreement [Finding #6436] [Finding #6450] [Finding #6484].

John Solly served as a DOGE-affiliated SSA staffer who submitted the formal request to copy the NUMIDENT to cloud storage on June 10–11, 2025 — four days after the Supreme Court ruling. Michael Russo, another DOGE-aligned CIO who preceded Moghaddassi at SSA, provided the initial June 25 authorization for Solly's upload request [Finding #6431] [Finding #6397].

Charles Borges served as SSA Chief Data Officer and filed the whistleblower disclosure with the Office of Special Counsel on August 26, 2025, specifically naming the NUMIDENT cloud transfer. He resigned August 29. Greg Pearre, SSA's career IT chief, was physically removed from his office for refusing to execute the Death Master File additions [Finding #6407] [Finding #6476].

Antonio Gracias, a Tesla and SpaceX board member, served as a DOGE operative at SSA during the same period [Finding #5985].

open_questions: The encrypted, password-protected file transmitted by a DOGE SSA member to DHS on March 3, 2025 — containing names and addresses of approximately 1,000 people — remained inaccessible to SSA's CIO as of January 2026. What was the file's contents, who at DHS received and opened it, and was any action taken on the data? The file's transmission predates the Cloudflare window by four days and appears to be a separate exfiltration channel. [Finding #6432] [Finding #6404]

The Voter Data Agreement was signed by a DOGE SSA member on March 24, 2025. The advocacy group is identified in court records as unnamed. True the Vote is suspected but denies involvement. Court discovery motions by Democracy Forward were filed in January 2026 seeking depositions on DOGE data access. Has the identity of the contracting advocacy group been established through that discovery process? [Finding #6410] [Finding #6414]

The June 25, 2025 NUMIDENT upload to AWS was authorized by Michael Russo on that date; the Provisional ATO was not issued until July 15 by Moghaddassi. This means the database was in the cloud environment for 20 days before any formal authorization was issued. What access controls, if any, were in place during that 20-day window, and was any data queried, copied, or transmitted from the AWS environment before the ATO was issued? [Finding #6397] [Finding #6401] [Finding #6516]

The Peters HSGAC minority staff report assessed that DOGE operations likely violated the Privacy Act, E-Government Act, FISMA, and Federal Records Act. The DOJ filed a Notice of Corrections in January 2026 acknowledging prior misrepresentations to the court. Has the Inspector General of SSA opened a formal investigation, and has any criminal referral been made to DOJ under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act? [Finding #6408] [Finding #6414]

Moghaddassi emailed DeSantis's deputy chief of staff from a DHS email account in March 2025 requesting Florida voter registration data. The email was obtained via public records. Were there equivalent communications with officials in other states seeking voter roll data, and has the Hatch Act referral regarding this email been acted upon by the Office of Special Counsel? [Finding #6475] [Finding #6450]

The Death Master File additions included minors as young as 13 and used fabricated death dates. The partial reversal documented in subsequent SSA records left approximately 407 living immigrants' records still active in the DMF as of the NCTR reporting date. Have those remaining 407 records been corrected, and has any individual suffered documented harm — loss of benefits, account suspension, or denial of services — as a result of their fraudulent death record? [Finding #6476]

As of January 2026, SSA could not determine whether Cloudflare had deleted the data routed through its servers during March 7–17, 2025. Has Cloudflare produced records in response to the AFSCME litigation discovery, and what do those records show about data retention, queries, or onward transmission? [Finding #6404]
